items.body: Neram Pularumbol (“As The Dawn Breaks”) finds Sunken Cages pulling the rhythmic traditions of South India into an electronic vocabulary of bass, drones, and fractured club music. The album opens in celebratory, ebullient mode with “Kerala”, before “Elephant Dance” raises the tempo and “Idakka” takes a more synthetic path, processing patterns from the traditional hourglass-shaped Kerala drum. Breath soon becomes almost as important as rhythm. On “Darantee”, featuring Kuza, vocal exhalations and percussion give the music a physicality that draws on the agricultural and folk roots of South India. The connection with Kerala runs throughout the record, particularly through the collective force of its percussion traditions. “Drum and Flowers” imagines Chenda drums within a celebratory night dance, their increasingly animated rhythms rubbing against darker industrial sounds. “Athiraavile” — Malayalam for “early in the morning” or “at the break of dawn” — shifts the scene towards daybreak, combining an unprocessed Chenda melam pattern with heavy electronic beats and Rani Jambak’s incantatory voice. Throughout, traditional instruments remain clearly audible even as their rhythmic properties are stretched, fragmented and repositioned. The second half effectively takes that process apart again through a substantial series of remixes. “Drum and Flowers” alone appears in three new iterations: Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull its rhythmic framework in sharply different directions, at points veering towards acid, jungle and deconstructed club music. The source material consequently keeps changing hands and contexts, with each version exposing possibilities latent in the original. For all its electronic density, Neram Pularumbol eventually circles back towards the physical act of playing. “Kerala (Moki McFly Remix)” brings proceedings to an apt conclusion, returning percussion to a more tactile foreground and introducing distinctly jazzy, free-form leanings. The album begins and ends with “Kerala”, but the intervening transformations ensure that the return doesn’t feel quite like arriving at the same place. photo by Mike Vanemon To find out more about the production process for the album, we got in touch directly with Ravish Momin (aka Sunken Cages). The liner notes to Neram Pularumbol use resynthesis not simply as an electronic process but as a metaphor for taking culture apart into its constituent elements and putting it together differently, in opposition to the idea of tradition as something “frozen, solidified and sanctified”. That does seem particularly audible on Neram Pularumbol, where South Indian instruments and rhythmic languages are present but rarely allowed to function as straightforward markers of heritage. What exactly are you trying to preserve when you dismantle and reconstruct a tradition in this way, and at what point does transformation become more important than recognisability? Does this also connect with what you have described elsewhere as “resynthesizing the traditional” and decolonising conventional ideas of so-called global music? Thanks for this great question! The best analogy to start with is to think of making a photocopy of a photocopy. Even 8-10 generations of copies later, they do not resemble the original, get distorted and warped, and perhaps even a new narrative emerges. This process itself is of deep interest to me and what I’m hoping to preserve. When I think of a rhythm I’ve learned in the past, it’s more about how I’m recalling it in the moment, with all the unconscious inspirations and changes that get added over time- to be left with a transformation that’s an impression, an organic reimagining- similar to what happens to our own memories over time. Furthermore, I’m taking these ‘resynthesized patterns’ and placing them in a new framework of synths, drones, and other electronic elements that I’ve absorbed, to create a new global-music that simply doesn’t rely on invoking the past. I need to be careful to add that all this does not mean a blatant disrespect of the culture and tradition, but to be left with recognizable elements-like the sounds and basic structure of a pattern- in an arrangement that may be unfamiliar. That’s where the decolonizing takes shape. Music is predicated on a dynamic process of growth and evolution, yet too often non-western artists are expected to be performative of their culture, and their use of contemporary technologies or drawing inspirations from western genres is considered disingenuous. Gatekeeping and branding from western ethnomusicologists and curators has a long problematic history, but I’ll leave that discussion for another time Neram Pularumbol is particularly rooted in the musical traditions of Kerala, from the title itself to “Idakka”, named after the hourglass-shaped drum associated with Kerala’s temple music. Yet you don’t present these traditions ethnographically or attempt to reproduce them faithfully: their rhythmic and timbral characteristics are broken apart and absorbed into electronics, bass and club structures. Which particular Kerala musical traditions, instruments or rhythmic practices fed into this album, and what is your own relationship to them? Are there elements that you consciously wanted to retain in recognisable form, and others that you felt could only remain alive by being transformed? Hopefully my previous response lends some insight to this question as well. To elaborate, I’ve always found group drumming to be powerful, an action of resistance and solidarity as well as of spiritual significance. Particularly, I was mesmerized by music performances known as Chenda melam in which hundreds of artists sync and perform together during temple festivals in Kerala. The drums native to Kerala, like the Chenda, Idakka and Elathalam, also have markedly different timbres/sonorities from the North-Indian drums such as Tabla and Dhol to which one may be accustomed to hearing. While I’m originally from South India (Hyderabad) myself, I currently split my time between Brooklyn and Philadelphia. I did not grow up in Kerala, India, but I wanted to think about what a meaningful recreation of those rituals into my own worldview, that was culturally respectful as well, would represent. For example, On “Drum and Flowers,” I created a narrative with shifting tempos where the Chenda drum is used in a celebratory night dance, after the workers have come home. A multitude of drums lead the celebrations, shedding industrial grime for synchronized movements that quicken, a shared bodily memory of ancestral resistance and resilience. The song is punctuated with industrial textures and dark synth stabs that represent the rigor of factory-work. “Idakka,” the track to which you’d alluded earlier, runs the Idakka drum patterns through various delays and echo filters to create this cavernous rhythmic feel where machine-like sounds are also ever-present. Here the traditional elements are drastically transformed and chopped up, signifying a not-too-distant future where machines threaten to take over humanity. On “Athiraavile,” which features the Indonesian producer/vocalist Rani Jambak, I actually used a clean / unprocessed Chenda melam pattern on top of heavy electronic beats. Here, Rani lends a shaman-like call to prayer- not belonging to any specific religious denomination- where people gather to play drums at dawn. The second half of the album effectively allows other artists to take your rhythmic material apart again. “Drum and Flowers” is especially revealing because Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull the same source towards very different rhythmic and electronic environments, while Masma Dream World and Moki McFly produce two strikingly different versions of “Kerala” and Kush Arora makes “Idakka” considerably harsher and more propulsive. You have said that these collaborators were chosen partly through relationships you have built with artists around the world who approach tradition as something mutable rather than fixed. When you heard the finished remixes, did any of them reveal something in your own compositions that you hadn’t realised was there? And does handing the music over to artists from such different cultural and musical contexts become another stage of the album’s idea of resynthesis? The remixes were as much a part of the album as the tracks. And a resounding yes to your observation of having these remixes represent a further reshaping of the source-material, as multiple layers of resynthesis now exist Each artist brought their respective cultural background, musical aesthetic and production style to the table. Back during the pandemic lockdown in 2020, I’d actively sought out remote collaborations with artists in different corners of the globe. I do want to emphasize that it was also important for me to support women artists, do my part to highlight them in a male-dominated electronic music scene. Over the years, I’ve maintained my goal of building a musical community with diverse collaborators who all take musical risks and blend the traditional to the digital in their own practice. As an artist with a remix track-record of my own (Babani Sound System, Batida’s Ikoqwe, Depeche Mode, dragonchild and Thollem), I’ve spent a lot of time listening to a given track to quickly hone in on elements that resonated with my aesthetic- whether it was a vocal phrase, a melody or a rhythmic motif. The objective was to take apart the original track and re-stitch it back together highlighting that chosen element, in ways that wouldn’t be predictable. El Kontessa added a doumbek pattern to the underlying rhythm and made it feel like it was always there, as if South Indian and Egyptian musicians jammed all the time. Masma Dream World took the drone elements of “Kerala” which I’d intentionally layered heavily, to create a very cinematic track with a stripped down minimal beat. Weldroid’s acid synths and bit-crushed elements gave the track a dance music of the future energy. Lila Tirando a Violeta removed my rhythmic elements entirely and energized the track with a Jungle vibe. Moki Mc Fly seemed to instinctively grasp my AACM past- which was grounded in their ancient to the future motto- and brought an acoustic Free-Jazz tribute to the Art Ensemble of Chicago to his remix. Neram Pularumbol means “As The Dawn Breaks”, while the name Sunken Cages itself has a much darker environmental origin: you have described the “sunken cage” as an image of something once held captive becoming submerged by rising waters, reflecting your background in environmental engineering and longstanding concern with climate change. Yet this record often feels less apocalyptic than that image suggests: despite the drones, industrial textures and moments of considerable darkness, there is movement, colour and a sense of emergence. What does “dawn” mean within this record? Is it intended as a counterweight to the darker implications of Sunken Cages, or do you see destruction, transformation and renewal as parts of the same process? For the past few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the duality of the nature of water, as a source of survival and also as one of destruction. While there is a sense of hopelessness that comes from realizing that some of the impacts of climate-change are irreversible, there is also hope in focussing on environmentally sustainable practices. Rather than thinking of dawn as a counterweight to the bleakness of the overarching climate narrative, I wanted to leave its symbolism ambiguous. In other words, we can meet the dawn feeling powerless or prepare to transform our future for preservation. On a broader level, the choice still doesn’t seem to have been made. As far as the tracks go, I play with the tension between the forces of darkness and rejuvenation- with the industrial sounds/textures on the verge of overpowering the ancient rhythms and chants, which signify our humanity, and certainly different tracks allude to different outcomes of that struggle. PS. Since this interview took place, Momin has released Morning Birds and Distant Drums, a new album with Haitian “soundchemist” Val Jeanty as Turning Jewels Into Water. Taking the AACM credo “Ancient to the Future” as a guiding principle, the record brings their Indian and Haitian lineages into a kinetic dialogue with improvisation and contemporary electronics. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Logan — The ambient, coolly nostalgic opening sequence of Geogaddi indicates the record's direction. Adjusting to the full album required some acclimation after years of listening to Music Has the Right to Children, but many elements appealed to me right away. Taking some distance from the debut allowed this strange, isolated world to make sense."Music Is Math" and "1969" rely on steady, ticking beats reminiscent of the D�sseldorf electronic scene, but with an uneasy feeling underneath. Further into the tracklist, pieces like "The Beach at Redpoint", "Gyroscope", and "Alpha and Omega" shift toward a darker Krautrock friction. The record relies on hypnotic, repetitive loops rather than traditional musical showmanship, focusing on old-sounding, distorted analog textures.My first favourite was clearly Music Has the Right to Children, which I found immediately accessible, followed by The Campfire Headphase, though I still loved Geogaddi during that era. However, it was only after Inferno came out that I deeply loved the final three albums, and the early material became more distant to me. This record is more like a 4.5 for me, though it gets a rounded-down 4 for Prog Archives purposes. Geogaddi is a strong exercise in sound design, but it remains a step below those late-career masterpieces for me. Inferno, The Campfire Headphase, and Tomorrow's Harvest mean the most to me these days, but all of Boards of Canada's albums I consider to be masterpieces in their own ways.Key tracks for me: "The Beach at Redpoint" and "Music is Math".

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — For far too long, Tim Smith remained the archetype of the artist misunderstood in his own country and simply ignored everywhere else?the leader of a visionary and essential band that deserved more recognition. Yet we are rediscovering music of undeniable quality and originality. Over time, CARDIACS has evolved from an unclassifiable oddity to a legendary band, recognized by virtually everyone (including the British press, which is no stranger to belated revivals) as a major piece of the global rock puzzle.*On Land And In The Sea* follows in the footsteps of its predecessor (*A Little Man And A House ...*, 1988), offering art-rock laced with frenzied madness, but this time without the element of surprise and with, in its first half, a more pronounced "prunk" vibe?the merry band having saved the best for last with "Buds and Spawn," a psychedelic anthem that could have been dreamed up in 1968 by a Syd Barrett even more unhinged than usual; and above all "The Everso Closely Guarded Line," a grandiose psycho-symphonic epic owed in part to Drake, which moves forward through an electric haze to the sounds of solemn keyboards. Sarah's sudden departure in the spring of 1989 (she would continue to collaborate sporadically with Tim Smith for a few more years) and, above all, that of William D. Drake two years later marked the end of an era. Drake was not replaced, and Tim Smith took sole charge of the keyboards, which were henceforth less prominent.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Is CARDIACS a progressive rock band? The question, which may have sparked debate at one time, seems obsolete today. All we can say is that singer and guitarist Tim Smith?the band's longtime leader, its heart, mind, and soul, and now more than ever regarded as an exceptional English artist, more than five years after his passing?is a child of the vibrant prog universe that truly lives up to its name. He himself cited among his countless influences such legendary names as Genesis, Faust, Can, Gong, Zappa, and Gentle Giant?a fact confirmed by the album *A Little Man And A House And The Whole World Window*.From the very introduction of the excellent new version of the track "A Little Man and a House," it becomes clear that this album will be on an entirely different level than *Seaside*, their previous album released in 1983. The compositions date back to the previous three years, but the production is much richer than on *Seaside* and in no way tainted by the typical sound of the '80s. Musically, it's a true leap forward, with arrangements of unprecedented richness ("The Icing on the World"), sometimes bordering on unnecessary excess ("The Breakfast Line," saved by its impressive grand finale). The significant contribution of William D. Drake's keyboards (who joined the band in late 1983) is no small part of this, as the musician displays a boundless imagination that rivals Tim's. Drake also co-wrote two of the album's most progressive tracks: "I'm Eating in Bed," which appears as a bonus track?a surreal little nursery rhyme that could easily have fit on *Nursery Cryme* or *Foxtrot*; and "The Whole World Window," which closes the album in a rather unexpected way, bringing CARDIACS closer to King Crimson's *In The Court* with heavy use of mellotron, piano, and bombastic organ, thereby convincing us once and for all that this is one of the most important prog works of 1988.

items.body: Review by Lewian — It is somewhat frustrating about rock from the old communist GDR (East Germany) that the possibilityof censorship didn't only affect the lyrics but apparently also had an impact on the music itself.People were strongly discouraged to think outside the box, and also to sound outside the box. Soproper innovation was very hard to find if at all. Everyone apparently wanted to (or had to) soundnice and civilised. In the 70s it was possible to play harder rock music if it clearly referenced,copied or covered rock'n roll and blues from the west as this was seen as anti western establishmentrebellion and therefore OK (at least at a certain time point), but rebellion against the ownconditions of life in the east wasn't allowed. This also meant that anything more aggressive anddark couldn't be done in innovative ways and couldn't directly relate to the musicians' daily life,seriously affecting creativity. Any opposition had to be subtle, often covered by nice melodicmusic, often enough straight and easy to listen to, and often of little attraction to the proglistener 40 years or so later. Lyrics were often poetic and indirect. Innovation could be brought in best by incorporating classical musicinfluences, as Electra and Stern Meissen did, and Lift to some extent. I believe that the situationfor creativity was really more problematic in the GDR than it was for example in Poland, Hungary andthe Czech Republic, but I can't know for sure (certainly there was a more lively jazz scene in thelatter countries).Lift's Meeresfahrt is one of the best albums to negotiate these conditions. It is in factastonishing that the major theme of longing for travel and far away countries on this album didn'tcreate problems with the censors, as far as I know, given that most people were not allowed totravel outside the eastern communist block of countries. The album is very melodic indeed, the band doesn't rock hard (OK a little bit in very few places),but they are good at what they do. Most arrangements are dominated by the two very good keyboarders.The vocals are also attractive, clean and melodic. The opener "Wir fahrn uebers Meer" is an exampleof copying western blues rock. Maybe the band used this to distract the censors, because in my viewit is by far the weakest track. This is followed by the extremely beautiful "Nach Sueden" ("GoSouth"). Not the proggiest track, but featuring a wonderful melody, a strong keyboard part, andlyrics on migrating birds that probably expressed the longing of many young people in the GDR butwere seemingly (and surprisingly) innocent enough for the censors to let the band get away withthis. A highlight!"Scherbenglas" is an example for the classical influence, using only a string section and voice. Norock at all but interesting and not bad. "Tagesreise" has an epic melody and works well asrecommendation piece for the prog fan with some contrasts and several sections. The second highlightof the album.On the B-side, "Meeresfahrt" (something like "Journey at Sea") is the longest track. It developsslowly from calm keyboards into a mostly instrumental journey featuring the keyboarders andsaxophonist in particular. This is surely enjoyable even though it may be a bit too long for what itis. "Sommernacht" is a calm good night song referencing traditional singing. It works well asending, even though not very interesting from the instrumental point of view. "Tagesreise" and "Meeresfahrt" hold most interest from the prog point of view, but the album hasvery nice elements also elsewhere if you are into melodic rock. It has light influences fromclassical music, jazz and blues. It has good variety but also comes over as consistent featuring acharacteristic style, particularly the melodies and keyboards. The most similar band I can think of is Novalis. Personally I'd rank this as thesecond best GDR prog/art rock album (after Stern Meissen's Reise zum Mittelpunkt des Menschen). 3.7stars.Sadly, few months after the release of this album in 1978, band members Henry Pacholski and GerhardZachar died in a traffic accident and the band would never be the same anymore.

I've never fully gotten onboard withCream, and maybe it's Eric Clapton that's the component that doesn't quite land for me, becausebetween Ginger Baker's work elsewhere and now this I can say I'm more impressed with the other Creammembers' solo fare than Clapton's.What you get here is bluesy art rock with brilliant bass lines and poetic lyrics by Pete Brown. Somesongs on here ended up travelling widely, with Mountain, Colosseum, and Greenslade covering farelike Theme From An Imaginary Western or Rope Ladder To the Moon; others definitely qualify as deepcuts. Either way, well worth exploring.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Quivira?the legendary name of a city of gold, forever sought but never found!It is also the concept behind an album by Lisa LaRue, who shines on keyboards and piano.1. (Intro) "The Coming Of The Spaniards" offers a symphonic, solemn, and majestic opening?a melody that stops you in your tracks. The choirs, the piano, the very essence of the music?simply perfect.2. "The Benefits Of Breathing Quietly" follows, featuring Vangelis-esque tones?sublime, with a distant, Native American-inspired breeze. Jake's vocals flirt with the style of Big Big Train; in short, top-tier stuff. The synth kicks in, riding over violin-like tones; it's simple yet beautiful, with hints of Alan Parsons?nothing but quality here.3. "The Plains? Truth" features a slow, drifting violin in "space-folk" mode?an airy instrumental interlude?concluding with an Andalusian acoustic touch that remains captivating throughout.4. "Quivira Bound" places the keyboard center stage; Jake casts a spell with his distinctive voice?not the late John, certainly, but his vocals are pure prog. It's an 80s-style ballad with a cheerful air; Lisa brings out a smaller synth before a Southern-rock/Cherokee guitar spirit floods the room with bewitching notes, with John embracing his role as an ex-Korgis member. A stereo finale blends the organ with the crystalline piano.5. "Moving Forward" reminds me of Solstice, featuring a jazzy-folk sound where Joe's violin engages in a musical duel. KANSAS is definitely present here after all, and the keyboards blend perfectly for one of the album's surprising detours.6. "The Turk/Follow The Wind" follows with organ, piano, and violin?sampled or not? That is the question. The drums aren't credited, implying they are programmed, which takes a bit of the shine off the album. Otherwise, it's a fine, energetic track that would have been a hit in the 70s! The cinematic ending puts my mind at ease.7. "Nothing Is Everything" marks the second half of the album?Side B. It has that KANSAS vibe again, with plenty of piano; softer yet dynamic, it feels like an 80s tune?over 40 years old; is it impossible to invent something new these days? Anyway, at times I hear ALAN PARSONS in "Andalusian mode"?it's a strange sensation.8. "Carved From The Sun," with its warm organ, reminds me of SHADOW GALLERY?that's just how it is. The velvety keyboard work lets the track drift along a smooth, seamless melodic path?paradoxically so.9. "Kicking Rocks" arrives, driven by a catchy guitar and a heavy riff; then it settles back down for a repeat performance.10. "Prelude To Anywhere/Weekend Conquistadors"... is it the spellbinding piano, the violin, or the synth? A beautiful ballad assaulted by John's hard-rocking riff, with the piano returning to sweep away any lingering heaviness. A masterful battle between the two instruments?top-tier stuff?with Jake setting things on fire, as does the PROTO-KAW-style vocal.11. "Still Breathing," with notes that recall TEARS FOR FEARS?that's just how it is. The final track; instead of leaving me breathless, it fills me up. A ballad?a lament balancing tenderness and emotion?featuring a violin? a keyboard? building to a dreamlike crescendo that drifts away on the musical breeze. A touch of Alan Parsons once again highlights the profound musicality of this final, spellbinding track. Off you go, steed?scram!QUIVIRA: symphonic progressive rock; a modern myth and vision of our troubled society set to music; melodic instrumental prog with occasional vocals?very good, yet it also tends to go in circles. Mr. Cadbury really shouldn't have wandered in.(3.75)

items.body: Harry Birch wrote “Don’t Give Up” while he was drinking himself under and his mother was dying of bone cancer. “This song saved me,” he says. He wrote it for her. The music pulls against all that: warm bass, guitar ringing bright over it, the tempo unhurried. Only the first line gives it away, Birch calling himself “a whiskey walking junkie”. Halfway through the song, he hands a verse to Lunda, a French-Congolese singer working in soul and indie rock. The chorus asks for time to put a broken life back together: “Please don’t give up on me / ‘Cause oh on our love we can revive / the pieces of our life…” Birch is Kaya Street, the Bristol project he writes, sings and produces. He formed it in 2014 as a ten-piece soul band, broke it up in early 2024 to get into the studio properly, then rebuilt it at the end of that year around live horns, drums and electronics. Juno-winning Toronto producer Dubmatix is producing the next Kaya Street album. “Don’t Give Up” stands apart from the afrobeat he usually works in, and from the political songs that come with it. items.body: Winter Sect have discovered one of goth’s better-kept secrets: graveyards can be funny places. Not funny in the sitcom sense, unless your sitcom happens to involve velvet sleeves, low fog, marble angels, and a bass player turning cemetery dirt into a dance floor, but funny in the grand old rock-and-roll sense that the concept of memento mori has always looked a little less terrifying once somebody places a wreath of backbeat on the coffin. Made up of Sister Ex alumna Claudia Neuman on bass and vocals, guitarist Anthony Piazza, keyboardist and vocalist Heather Wayward, and drummer Darryl J. Dardenne, the DC/Baltimore group have previously favored the colder end of Gothic psychedelia and glam rock. Graveyard Girl, however, loosens the corset. Funk, garage rock, indie pop and even bossa nova slip into the bloodstream, bringing a loose, easy groove beneath the song’s ’60s pop whimsy while the band keeps one boot planted firmly in post-punk soil. Neuman’s bass is responsible for the initial crime, strutting around with the casual confidence of someone who has found the liquor cabinet during a wake. Wayward’s keyboards add splashes of color around Piazza’s guitar, while Dardenne keeps the song moving with a lightness that gives its cemetery imagery room to grin. The melody has the cheeky charm of a vintage pop single, its tuneful bounce making the invitation to wander among the graves sound suspiciously like a proposition for a Sunday afternoon date. Siouxsie and the Banshees, March Violets, Strange Boutique and more hover somewhere in the family tree, although Winter Sect sound especially amused by the possibilities of their own material here. According to Wayward, that playful turn happened almost accidentally during rehearsal: “The song pretty much started with Claudia grooving out on a bass line,” she says. “It was catchy and I thought let’s do something completely different and not so serious and macabre. First the hook was discovered and we built from there. So with that funk of a groove my mind started walking. Where? Through the graveyard of course. It came together in a cool way and a little twist at the end just makes it fun.” That sense of fun carries into the video, which sends the band wandering through the necropolis in slow motion among candles, veils and fog. Somebody communes with the departed, everybody looks appropriately dressed for the occasion, and the solemn machinery of Gothic imagery gains a sly little wink. You half expect one of the headstones to start keeping time. Watch the video for Graveyard Girl below: Winter Sect began in late 2023 when California native Neuman and Piazza formed the project around feedback-heavy goth, New Wave, industrial and psychedelic influences. Mystic Twin and Haunted House followed in 2024, with Say Goodbye appearing in 2026. Graveyard Girl, taken from the forthcoming EP Offering, suggests Winter Sect have figured out that darkness becomes far more interesting when somebody remembers to leave room for mischief and a tune you can hum on the way home. Listen to Graveyard Girl below and order the single here. items.body: An ache moves forward He steps back I step forward It all turns black He steps forward I step back Some relationships develop their own terrible choreography: one person advances, the other retreats, and a moment of contact sends both back through the same steps. On Annihilate, underground post-industrial producer and vocalist Lana Del Rabies gives that exhausted dance a setting of metallic percussion, dissonant strings, and voices that seem to drift through the walls. The prospect of closeness carries a threat of disappearance, as though reaching for another person might cost you the outline of yourself. Released through her own Feral Crone Recordings, the single revisits the gothic industrial territory of her 2023 album STREGA BEATA. Among her most accessible recordings to date, Annihilate brings its melody into clearer view within a dense, unsettling arrangement, with echoes of mid-career Nine Inch Nails, early Chelsea Wolfe, Dead Can Dance, and Godflesh. Written and produced by Lana Del Rabies, the track features bass, guitar, and additional instrumentation from Zach Wise, formerly of experimental black metal band Hissing. Deeply reverberant string tones open the song, their discord setting the room askew before a soft metallic beat begins carrying it forward. Creaking noises punctuate the haze, while thudding distortion stays buried beneath the mix, suggesting a heartbeat accelerating at the approach of something unwelcome. Her singing is soft, breathy, and eerily close; farther away, wails stretch across the recording like cries attempting to reach the living. The whole thing suggests a deserted Victorian factory, its decaying rooms still occupied by machinery and something considerably harder to identify. That dusty, corroded atmosphere recalls the gothic industrial aesthetics of the 1990s, with every small sound acquiring an uncomfortable physical presence. The lyrics begin with images converging in reverse and a moment suspended in time. From there, the exchange becomes a sequence of opposing movements: his withdrawal prompts her advance, his approach sends her backward. “Push pull fade” reduces the relationship to its recurring mechanism. Hearing her name briefly promises recognition, but the next attempt at contact leaves her grasping in vain. By the time the title enters the refrain, desire reads as a force capable of wearing away the person who feels it. Directed and edited by Lana Del Rabies/Sam An, the video translates that instability into grainy woodland footage, overlapping figures, and close-ups that dissolve before they can offer much certainty. Pale dresses and fabric catch the light against dense foliage; raised arms, blurred faces, and bodies close to the ground recur through successive layers of exposure. Black-and-white images give way to smeared color, turning the setting into something resembling a damaged reel of folk horror. The footage was shot by Jane Slater, whose video credits include Dildox, Brood Faye, and Sacred Skin, and Vox Porter of Sleek Teeth. Watch the video for Annihilate below: Lana Del Rabies began with early experiments sampling female pop musicians into noise tracks, a practice reflected in the project’s name. An has since developed a body of work spanning industrial music, gothic electronics, and experimental heaviness, examining human brutality and the prospect of apocalypse. Her recordings have earned attention from The Quietus, Metal Hammer, and Anthony Fantano, while her live performances have taken her to festivals including Roadburn, Coldwaves, Sled Island, Prepare the Ground, Northwest Terror Fest, and Soulcrusher. She has toured with Author & Punisher, 3TEETH, Pharmakon, JPEGMAFIA, and John Wiese, and opened shows for artists including clipping., Midwife, HEALTH, and Bell Witch. In 2025, An founded the art-focused label Feral Crone Recordings and released Le Temps Viendra and Omnipotent Fuck. She is currently working on a studio record with former members of Hissing, due in 2027. Listen to Annihilate below and order the single here. items.body: Dreams may be among the strangest territories available to us. Each night, the mind constructs worlds without asking permission from physics, geography, biography, or common sense. We meet people who never existed, return to places that vanished years ago, fall in love with strangers, lose ourselves, recover ourselves, and wake carrying the emotional residue of events that never occurred. There is something almost miraculous in this private universe, because within it we are briefly released from the limits imposed by circumstance. Thought offers a similar freedom. We can imagine nearly anything, even when reality permits us to accomplish only a fraction of it. For Venus Volcanism, the Iceland-based project of Crete-born vocalist, musician, and producer Rena Rasouli, dreams become both refuge and research subject. Her new song, “Dreams,” inhabits the uncertain region between waking life and the private worlds that continue behind our eyes. Rasouli created the song exactly one year ago as the first snow settled across the peaks surrounding Siglufjörður, Iceland’s northernmost town. She keeps a journal beside her bed, recording complete dreams when possible and preserving stray images when that is all sleep leaves behind. Before sleeping, she gives herself a small invocation: “As I close my eyelids and sleep takes me, gently or not, please show me something that will help me understand myself a little better.” Dreams drifts somewhere between dark pop, ambient composition, experimental electronics, and neoclassical music, with affinities to This Mortal Coil, Julee Cruise, Penelope Trappes, and Zola Jesus. Rasouli’s voice occupies the center while drones, synthesizers, arpeggiated figures, and suspended textures create an unstable sense of location. Beauty and unease coexist. The song seems to hover between desire imagined and desire remembered. Its love story belongs to an imaginary lover, though imagination hardly makes the emotion less consequential. Desperation, longing, idealization, and obsession can become perfectly real experiences even when their object remains beyond reach. “Have you ever found yourself dreaming with your eyes open? I honestly don’t know how many times I have done it while diving into Icelandic pools,” says Rasouli. “Especially during winter, I feel like I am balancing somewhere between the conscious and the unconscious, and sometimes I don’t even know how the day has passed. I am and I am not. I exist and I do not exist. I do everything I am supposed to do; I move through the day as I should, but if you know me well enough, you might see it in my eyes: I am somewhere in between.” This suspended condition also governs the video, directed by Tassos Gkoletsos with help from friends and members of the Siglufjörður community. Northern Iceland’s long winter darkness turns ordinary routines into strange repetitions: tending plants, bathing, working, exercising, moving through familiar rooms while another existence unfolds internally. “During those months, I always find myself somewhere in between,” Rasouli continues. “I do everything I need to do and I’m relatively functional, but everything feels like autopilot. At the same time, another scene is taking place inside my head. I dream and imagine other things while going through the ordinary routines of everyday life, like watering my plants, having my bath, working, and going to the gym.” Perhaps this is why Dreams feels so intimate. Rasouli treats imagination as a parallel dimension of daily existence, one without measurable coordinates yet capable of altering everything that happens after we return. Watch the video for Dreams below: Listen to Dreams below and order the single here. items.body: Lift the veil, see what I’ve become An exoskeletal pantheon Born again from bone and breath To spread the living gospel of death On Tears for the Dying‘s blistering new gothic track Devour Me, Adria Stembridge drags the band back toward its earlier roots with a slower, heavier gait, then breaks that crawl apart with abrupt tempo changes that make the song feel unstable beneath your feet. Stembridge handles drum machine, guitar, bass, and vocals, building the track from dark guitar figures, blunt low-end pressure, and drums that move with the patience of something following you home. Her vocals hang above it all in a cold echo, less concerned with theatrical grandstanding than with letting the words rot in the air for a second before the next image lands. You can hear Bauhaus in the skeletal guitar work, Alien Sex Fiend in the queasy theatricality, and PiL and Fields of the Nephilim in the sense that somebody has wandered far enough from civilization to start inventing a religion. That religious impulse becomes central once the lyrics start opening the trapdoor. Stembridge draws from cosmic horror, but the terror here feels brutally physical. A solitary figure encounters an impossible swarm, loses control of the body piece by piece, and becomes host to something that treats flesh as raw material. Bones break. Insects burrow. The victim survives only in the technical sense, gradually becoming an alien deity whose transformation has erased whatever person existed before. The nastiest idea arrives afterward: worship. What begins as predation becomes conversion, and the ruined body becomes scripture. Consumption, reproduction, faith, and extermination collapse together until divinity itself starts looking like another parasitic infection. There is something wonderfully foul about that conception of godhood, especially coming from a band whose Southern gothic deathrock has long carried radical queer politics alongside its horror imagery. Authority here comes crawling out of meat. The slower passages give those images room to breathe before the faster sections shove everything toward panic. That contrast is crucial. Speed alone would turn the song into pursuit; the deliberate sections make you wait for whatever is chewing through the floorboards. By the final transformation, cosmic horror has lost every trace of abstraction. Infinity sprouts mandibles, theology breeds larvae, and salvation becomes a forced rebirth inside a body that has been converted into temple, nursery, and weapon. items.body: The screams of children, far away Echo in this perfect day A perfect society becomes considerably harder to admire once somebody explains who has been paying for it. In Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas, an entire city’s happiness depends upon the suffering of a single child, an arrangement its citizens learn to accept as the price of their good fortune. There is plenty of room for horror in that cheerful consensus, especially once the people benefiting from it begin explaining why things simply have to be this way. Bologna’s La Mano Sinistra, whose name means “the left hand” in Italian, take up that ugly bargain on their debut single, Unnecessary Perfection. The track introduces Omelas, a seven-track concept album due November 6, 2026, through Bat-Cave Productions, translating Le Guin’s ethical dilemma into gothic rock with enough melodic momentum to carry its uncomfortable questions straight onto the dancefloor. A heartbeat rhythm opens the track, its alternating accents pressing against sustained, cold synthesizer tones before a thick, low-slung bassline sends everything forward. Guitar and electronics give the melody a generous sweep while Davide Sacco sings with the decadent authority of a frontman who can make a warning sound almost inviting. The combination brings to mind The Danse Society around their Heaven Is Waiting era, with something of Children on Stun and Brotherhood of Pagans in the vocal delivery and the way the instruments lock together. The guitar break ascends and descends through the melody, supplying an exhilarating lift while sustaining the chill of the surrounding synths. When Sacco’s voice returns alongside it, a more romantic quality enters his timbre, adding a strange tenderness to the accusation. This is the kind of gothic rock that makes getting dressed to go out feel like the opening scene of an evening full of possibilities. For a song about the moral cost of everybody having a good time, it has a wicked talent for getting the evening started. The lyrics initially survey a population blessed with sharp minds, untouched lives, and the promise of a cure for all, while concealed currents move beneath that reassuring surface. Sacco’s recurring question, “What’s necessary, what is not,” unsettles the supposed inevitability of the arrangement. By the closing lines, children’s screams carry across the distance into the perfect day itself. Read alongside Le Guin’s story, that distance becomes part of the accusation: comfort depends upon keeping suffering far enough away to be tolerated, even when its beneficiaries know exactly what sustains their happiness. The band describe the single this way: “The paradox of perfection. A fast-paced, impactful track reflecting the fictitious tranquility of a society built upon the distant screams of the weakest.” The accompanying video gives that selective vision an effective visual counterpart. High-contrast black-and-white performance footage is crossed by horizontal bands that repeatedly interrupt faces, instruments, and the lyrics appearing on screen. Close-ups of hands working the strings alternate with Sacco at the microphone, while the bars make even the plainest words momentarily difficult to see. The treatment suggests an uncomfortable connection between an obstructed image and a society accustomed to accepting a partial view. Watch the video for Unnecessary Perfection below: La Mano Sinistra brings together Sacco on vocals and lyrics, Gianluca Lo Presti of Nevica on bass and electronics, and Giuseppe Lo Bue of Caron Dimonio on guitar and electronics. Sacco is also a co-founder of the contemporary theatre company ErosAntEros and artistic director of POLIS Teatro Festival, a background that gives the project’s theatrical character a clear foundation. Omelas grew out of Sacco’s stage production of The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas, performed by actress Eva Robin’s. Recorded at Loto Studio in Ravenna during the summer of 2025, the album develops its source material across seven chapters, addressing indifference, collective guilt, and the decision to abandon a prosperity built upon injustice for an uncertain life beyond it. Unnecessary Perfection is available on digital platforms. Omelas follows on November 6, 2026, via Bat-Cave Productions. items.body: Pygmy Children reissue their 1994 debut album “Malignant” as “Malignant: Redux” via Re:Mission Entertainment. The label describes the release as electro-industrial and EBM, with a release date of October 2, 2026. The original “Malignant” was recorded by Brian Roper and Pete Roper at Hit And Run Studios in Rockville, Maryland, between September and December 1993, and released on CD via Noname/Noslogan Productions in 1994 with an 11-track listing running from “Shock V3.1” through “File Regarding…”. “Malignant: Redux” adds five further tracks to that original running order. Re:Mission Entertainment has not published a description of what the “Redux” edition changes beyond its expanded tracklist; that detail is not yet confirmed. Malignant : Redux by Pygmy Children About Pygmy Children Pygmy Children is a US electro-industrial project built around Brian Roper and Pete Roper, active since the early 1990s. The duo released their debut album “Malignant” in 1994, followed by “Low Life Dream” in 1998. After a long gap, Pygmy Children returned through Re:Mission Entertainment with the EP “I Have No Name”, the single “Proof in Lies”, the “Signal Unknown” EP and the album “Coincidental Strategies”. “Malignant: Redux”, out October 2, 2026, revisits the project’s debut album more than three decades after its original release.

items.body: Tangent Strategy announces “Tristesse”, the project’s first new full-length album in five years. The album is inspired by the music of John Foxx and Die Form. “Tristesse” explores the fragile human psyche, where anger and melancholy sit next to each other. It looks at the defiance inside relationships, healthy and unhealthy alike, and the marks they leave on the people in them. Production-wise, the album takes a simpler approach than before, keeping the songs raw with deep bass, stark arrangements and noise running through the mix. “In an age of detachment, Tristesse is a reminder that attachment is no certain comfort either,” the project states. Tristesse by Tangent Strategy About Tangent Strategy Tangent Strategy was formed in 1996 by chd.y as an outlet for a musical outlook that grew more and more drawn to industrial music over the years. The project’s first full-length, “Revenant”, came out in November 2021 via EK Product. Since then, chd.y has released several EPs under the name and performed live in Tokyo. “Tristesse”, announced in 2026, is Tangent Strategy’s second full-length album.

items.body: Vampire Valentine release “Scarred & Sacred” on October 25, 2026 via Morella Records. The six-track EP is the UK darkwave and post-punk trio’s fourth release since signing to the label on January 15, 2026, following a run of singles, the “Pale Dawn” EP and their self-titled debut album this past August. Where the self-titled album was a complete statement of the band’s sound, “Scarred & Sacred” follows a single arc across its six tracks: sin, repentance and the reckoning that waits at the gate. “Scarred & Sacred is our sins repenting and facing your fate in the afterlife at the gate,” the band says. “We wanted six tracks that felt like one story, not six songs that happened to ship together. It starts calm and it does not stay that way.” Scarred & Sacred tracklist Scarred (instrumental) – an atmospheric, melodic intro that turns unsettling, setting up the EP. Broken Sins – a full-length track pairing darkwave production with post-punk revival. Talisman – the story of a lover placing a talisman with a dying partner to guide them to the other side. Lover Not A Biter (instrumental) – a hard-driven darksynth track. GORE! (instrumental) – a darksynth cut the band describes as built on 1980s horror soundtracks and visuals. Sacred – the title track and closer, a post-punk song ending on vocals from frontman Michael Longstaff. Credits Michael Longstaff handles lyrics and vocals, Kieron Wright plays bass and Tobias Cowen Pickard plays drums. Tony Gunk produced, composed, mixed and mastered all six tracks. Ricky Conover, who records as Forerunnerx, co-produced and co-composed “Scarred”, “Lover Not A Biter” and “GORE!”. Blake Carpenter plays guitar on “Broken Sins”, “Talisman”, “Lover Not A Biter” and “GORE!”. About Vampire Valentine Vampire Valentine is a darkwave and post-punk band from Newcastle upon Tyne, formed in October 2025 by producer Michael Longstaff and bassist/guitarist Kieron Wright, who connected through a mutual acquaintance, along with drummer Tobias Cowen Pickard. US producers Ricky Conover (Forerunnerx) and Tony Gunk handle production. The band draws on The Sisters of Mercy, Twin Tribes, She Past Away and Lebanon Hanover. They debuted on November 14, 2025 with the single “Porcelain”, backed with “Olivia”, which goth journalist Mick Mercer called an “Excellent Debut”. A second single, “Thorns”, followed on December 1, 2025. Vampire Valentine signed to Morella Records on January 15, 2026 and released their debut full-length album that August, having already shared the singles “In The Dark” and “Cutting Ties” from it. “Scarred & Sacred”, out October 25, follows as the band’s fourth Morella release in under a year.

items.body: Assemblage 23 releases “Believe (INHALT Remix)” on 2 October 2026 via Metropolis Records. The single reworks “Believe”, the opening track from Tom Shear’s tenth Assemblage 23 album “Null”, released in November 2025. The remix comes from US producer Matia Simovich, who records as INHALT. “In INHALT’s expert hands, this song has been transformed. It has one foot on the mid-’80s dancefloor and the other planted firmly in the future,” Shear says of the rework. Believe (INHALT Remix) by Assemblage 23 “Believe” first appeared on “Null”, which Shear promoted with a UK tour ahead of its release and a run of sold-out shows in Germany. He returns to Europe this October for further dates in Germany and Sweden, several of which are already sold out. “‘Believe’ is about a hope for better things, even with the state of the world as it is today,” Shear said when the song first came out. “We are responsible for making the kind of world we live in. In the face of bad times, sometimes the most subversive thing you can do is to have hope.” Assemblage 23 live dates, October 2026 20 October – Karlsruhe, Die Stadtmitte (Germany) 21 October – Oberhausen, Kulttempel (Germany) 22 October – Hamburg, Indra Musikclub (Germany) 23 October – Jönköping, SekktorF (Sweden) – sold out 24 October – Hannover, Subkultur (Germany) – sold out Remaining tickets are available through the Assemblage 23 website. About Assemblage 23 Assemblage 23 is the recording name of US producer and songwriter Tom Shear, active since the late 1990s. His debut album “Contempt” placed him at the front of the electro-industrial and Future Pop scene that took hold on underground dancefloors at the turn of the millennium. Side-Line interviewed Shear about his long career and songwriting process. “Null”, Shear’s tenth album as Assemblage 23, was announced for Metropolis Records and released on 7 November 2025, led by the single “Tolerate”. Shear’s lyrics have long dealt directly with difficult personal subjects, including suicide and depression, a directness that has built him a following that keeps him touring regularly. “Believe (INHALT Remix)”, out 2 October 2026, pairs the “Null” opener with a rework by Matia Simovich (INHALT) ahead of Assemblage 23’s latest run of European dates.

items.body: Test Dept and the Welsh performance company Brith Gof release “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” on 4 December 2026 via Artoffact Records. The set expands their 1989 album into a 3CD/1DVD box, alongside a separate red vinyl LP and a digital edition. “Gododdin” is based on Y Gododdin, the earliest surviving Welsh-language poem, written around 600 AD. It tells of 300 Celtic warriors who attacked 100,000 invading Angles and lost. Test Dept and Brith Gof first staged the piece as a live performance at an abandoned Rover car factory in Cardiff in December 1988, using 600 tons of sand, 50 trees and 30 wrecked cars on a set that flooded as the show went on. Further performances followed in 1989 in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. The original 1989 studio album was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios from Test Dept’s existing studio and field recordings, augmented with brass and wind courtesy of Brith Gof’s John E R Hardy and bagpipes from Alistair Adams. Paul Jamrozy’s voice runs alongside the Welsh-language vocals of Lis Hughes Jones. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” widens that original 7-track album with 19 tracks that have not previously been released. The first disc is a reworked version built from newly unearthed multitrack tapes of the early studio sessions, put together by Test Dept founder members Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy during the summer of 2026. The second disc carries a live recording from one of the 1989 performances, staged in a quarry in Polverigi, Italy. The DVD holds a documentary from the period, with live footage and interviews with performers, academics and other experts. Compiled by Test Dept with input from Brith Gof members Lis Hughes Jones, John E R Hardy and Heike Roms, the set was remastered by Paul Lavigne at Kontrast Mastering. It comes in a 5-panel ecopak with a 24-page booklet of archival imagery and writing, including an essay by author and Test Dept researcher Alexei Monroe. The artwork for both the box and the separate red vinyl LP was redesigned by Paul Jamrozy and Stefan Alt (ant-zen); the vinyl edition carries the original album plus one previously unreleased track and a printed insert. Ahead of the box set, Test Dept released the advance single “Gwr a Aeth Gatraeth / Prologue (Early Studio Sessions, Reworked 2026)” on 2 October 2026, available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” is the second in Test Dept’s ongoing series of archival reissues on Artoffact Records, who signed the band in 2025 for catalogue reissues and a new album. It follows the 4xCD “Industrial Overture: Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”, released a year earlier. Artoffact will also release new Test Dept material in 2027. A separate event ties into the reissue: Test Dept and Brith Gof take part in a discussion and Q&A about “Gododdin” at Chapter in Cardiff on 24 October, as part of the Experimentica festival’s 25th-anniversary programme. About Test Dept Test Dept formed in London in the early 1980s as an industrial music group built around live percussion on scrap metal and found objects. In 1988 and 1989, the band collaborated with the Welsh avant-garde theatre company Brith Gof on “Gododdin”, staging it first at an abandoned car factory in Cardiff and then on tour in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. The 1989 studio album version was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios. Test Dept returned to active release and performance in the 2020s. In 2025, the band signed to Artoffact Records for a series of catalogue reissues alongside a new studio album. The first of those reissues, the 4xCD “Industrial Overture: Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”, arrived in October 2025. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster”, out 4 December 2026, is the second. Current members Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy built new versions of the early “Gododdin” studio sessions for the reissue during the summer of 2026, working from recently unearthed multitrack tapes. Test Dept continue to tour, with confirmed UK and European dates running from October 2026 into the summer of 2027, and have a new studio album due via Artoffact in 2027. About Brith Gof Brith Gof is a Welsh performance company known for large-scale, site-specific theatre work that drew on Welsh history and language. Co-founded by figures including Mike Pearson, Lis Hughes Jones and Clifford McLucas, the company staged “Gododdin” with Test Dept in Cardiff in 1988, adapting the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin into a promenade performance inside a disused car factory. Hughes Jones, John E R Hardy and Heike Roms were directly involved in compiling “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” alongside Test Dept.

The nine-track record sat unfinished for years, surfacing only after a self-titled Sevit album filled the gap in 2024. “Requiem” runs nine tracks: Ode To A Requiem Beyond My Control Escape Dreamland In So Many Words It Must Be Berlin Until Sundown The Happy Crowd The Walls Are Closing In (Original Version) Re
items.body: Sevit released “Requiem”, a darkwave album the Dallas-area duo wrote as the follow-up to 2021’s “On The Edge Of A Darker Place,” on 1 October 2026. The nine-track record sat unfinished for years, surfacing only after a self-titled Sevit album filled the gap in 2024. “Requiem” runs nine tracks: Ode To A Requiem Beyond My Control Escape Dreamland In So Many Words It Must Be Berlin Until Sundown The Happy Crowd The Walls Are Closing In (Original Version) Requiem Requiem by Sevit Sevit have not detailed why the record was set aside, but the band summed up the gap in one line: “Maybe some records simply have to wait until the people who created them finally catch up with them.” Sevit’s ‘Requiem’ follows ‘On The Edge Of A Darker Place’ “Requiem” is out now on Bandcamp as a digital release. About Sevit Jackie Legos (vocals, guitar) and Cam B. (synths, programming) write and record Sevit from the Dallas, Texas area, where the duo formed in 2020 after both had played in earlier North Texas bands, including At Night and Pleasure Crisis. They issued the “A Darker Place” EP that same year and signed to Peru’s InClub Records that October. Sevit’s debut album, “On The Edge Of A Darker Place,” arrived in September 2021: thirteen tracks that draw on The Cure, Joy Division, Bauhaus and Siouxsie & The Banshees, played live by a five-piece band built around the Legos and Cam B. core. Jackie Legos has described the band’s lyrics as rooted in “poetry, and things that might have directly and indirectly crossed my path in life.” The duo wrote “Requiem” as that album’s direct sequel, then set it aside. A self-titled album filled the gap in 2024. “Requiem” finally surfaces, closing a chapter the band had otherwise left open.

items.body: Miss Construction returns with “This Is Crap”, a new EBM and industrial-electro album that pairs eleven new tracks with a reissue of the project’s 2008 debut. Out 27 November 2026 on Out Of Line as a 2CD digipak, it follows “Boys & Ladies”, the sixth single, released 30 September. Disc one holds the eleven new tracks: This Is Crap (Intro) 6666 Heiß Hate Spiel Mit Mir Back Again F.M.P. Boys & Ladies This Is War Bully Du This Is Crap by Miss Construction Disc two reissues “Kunstprodukt,” Miss Construction’s debut album, originally released 28 April 2008 on Fear Section. It adds two archival remixes to the original sixteen tracks: the title track remixed by Gintronic, and “Electro Beast” remixed by Dolls Of Pain. “Boys & Ladies” arrived as an official video through Out Of Line Music’s YouTube channel on 30 September, embedded below. Miss Construction’s road back to ‘This Is Crap’ “Boys & Ladies” caps a run of five singles that marked Miss Construction’s return: “Spiel Mit Mir” in October 2025, “Back Again” in December 2025, then “Heiß,” “Hate” and “F.M.P.” through 2026. “This Is Crap” is available to pre-order now through the Out Of Line shop and on Bandcamp. About Miss Construction Miss Construction began in 2008 as a side project of Chris Pohl, who had fronted Blutengel since 1996. Pohl brought in Gordon Mocznay as co-vocalist, and the pair debuted the project at Wave-Gotik-Treffen in Leipzig that year. Its opening statement was a cover of Terminal Choice’s “Totes Fleisch,” placed on the debut album “Kunstprodukt,” released 28 April 2008 on Fear Section, an Out Of Line sublabel. Pohl and Mocznay followed it with “United Trash – The Z Files” in November 2013. Between full-lengths, Miss Construction contributed remixes to Blutengel and Dance Or Die compilations between 2009 and 2011, including the “Awake The Machines” and “Industrial For The Masses” series, before the project went quiet for twelve years. Pohl revived Miss Construction in 2025. “Spiel Mit Mir” opened the comeback that October, “Back Again” followed in December, and “Heiß,” “Hate,” “F.M.P.” and “Boys & Ladies” continued it through 2026. “This Is Crap” closes that run of singles and gives “Kunstprodukt” its first reissue.

items.body: Corlyx released “The Holy Vampire” on 1 October 2026, the fourth single from “The Crimson Tapes,” the darkwave trio’s next album due in early 2027 on Out Of Line Music. Guitarist and producer Brandon Ashley made the track with singer Caitlin Stokes, who also directed and edited its companion video alongside Sereina Winters. Ashley called the track’s tone deliberate: “It’s also quite camp, which Corlyx is a huge fan of.” He placed it close to 2025’s “Purple Pain,” pairing dancefloor elements with a harder deathrock edge than that album. Corlyx’s ‘The Holy Vampire’ leads to ‘The Crimson Tapes’ “The Holy Vampire” is streaming now and available on Bandcamp. About Corlyx Corlyx call their sound “Death Pop,” a label singer Caitlin Stokes coined for a mix of 1980s post-punk and goth rock. The band started in Los Angeles, releasing its first single, “Starlet,” in February 2016, and now splits its time between the UK and Italy, where Stokes works with guitarist and producer Brandon Ashley and bassist Davide Rocco. Corlyx’s video for “Twist Like An Animal” arrived in 2019. The band announced the album “Blood In The Disco” in 2021 behind the single “Take Off Everything,” then returned in 2024 with “Zombie Kid” ahead of the double album “Purple Pain” the following year. Corlyx has toured Europe, the UK and the US with Lord Of The Lost, Massive Ego, Ashbury Heights, Blutengel and Twin Tribes. “Sweeter Than Blood,” “More Anarchy” and “Your Heart In The Serpent’s Mouth” preceded “The Holy Vampire” as the first three singles from “The Crimson Tapes.”

items.body: The Pixel Rain released “Glitching Sky” on October 2, 2026, the fourth and final advance single from the Southeast London act’s debut album, “A Sense of Danger,” due October 29 on Bandcamp, Spotify and other digital platforms. The track pushes vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Áron Siegler’s electronic side further forward, bringing futurepop and synthwave into the project’s established synthpop sound, with Siegler citing VNV Nation and Chvrches among the single’s reference points. At the center of the song is a character retreating from an unfulfilling reality into a virtual world where he can construct a more powerful version of himself. Siegler extends the idea beyond any specific technology or platform to a broader comment on how people seek distraction from anxiety, disappointment and everyday life. Siegler describes the retreat as carrying both sadness and absurdity: “The idea came from thinking about someone whose real life isn’t giving them very much, so they retreat into a virtual world where they can be whoever they want to be. There’s something quite sad about that, but also something a little ridiculous, so I wanted the story to have both sides to it. “I deliberately left the virtual world undefined because I think that kind of escape can take a lot of different forms. I’m certainly not outside of it myself. We all have things we disappear into when reality gets uncomfortable. “The music is quite fast and energetic, but the song itself takes its time building. That seemed to fit the idea: you don’t necessarily notice yourself getting drawn further and further into these little distractions until they’ve started taking up much more of your life than you intended.” The single arrives with a visualizer by Sophie Maria Vickers, built around the song’s virtual setting and digital imagery. Glitching Sky by The Pixel Rain On Bandcamp, “Glitching Sky” is bundled together with The Pixel Rain’s three earlier advance singles, “Last,” “A Sense of Danger” and “Sacrifice.” The single is also on Spotify and other major platforms. About The Pixel Rain The Pixel Rain is the solo project of vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Áron Siegler, originally from Hungary and now based in Southeast London. The project emerged from London’s underground scene with a self-titled debut EP in 2023, and mixes dark electronic and post-punk elements with guitar, electronics and industrial textures. The Pixel Rain released the first single from its forthcoming debut album, “Last,” on June 19, 2026, with a video shot in Hungary in which Siegler was joined on screen by Balázs Fűr, András Melles, Máté Breier and Máté Király-Gyeőry. The singles “A Sense of Danger” and “Sacrifice” followed over the summer, each previewing the album further. “Glitching Sky,” released October 2, 2026, is the fourth and final advance single before the debut album “A Sense of Danger” arrives on October 29, 2026. The album explores power, authority, consumerism and social unease through recurring post-apocalyptic and technological imagery.

items.album: Wrocław 2026
items.excerpt: On 1 October 2026, Nachtmahr chose Poland to open the longest and largest tour in the project’s history: three consecutive club dates in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the opening run before IMPERIVM continues further across Europe.
